newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Branson "very confident" of roundworld balloon trip.
newsitem.headline: Branson "very confident" of roundworld balloon trip.

text.p: Flamboyant British tycoon Richard Branson, after a weekend locked in the capsule of his giant balloon, was "very confident" on Sunday of making the first round-the-world trip by balloon.
"It's been very, very intensive, 12-14 hours a day in the capsule, so they are feeling very confident," spokeswoman Jackie McQuillan told Reuters.
"They have been locked in the capsule again all morning, training on equipment, satellite communications and so on."
The team was returning to London later on Sunday to be on 72-hours notice standby, waiting for ideal weather in Morocco to take them straight into the southerly sub-tropical jet stream.
"The earliest would be the end of next week," she said.
Branson and one co-pilot Per Linstrand arrived late on Friday in this southern Moroccan city. Hang-gliding champion Rory McCarthy, the other co-pilot, arrived on Saturday.
"It's an epic adventure," project manager David Partridge said at the military base at the foot of the Atlas Mountains.
Branson, the 45-year-old boss of Virgin group of companies was thwarted last January by constant bad weather from making the attempt in a 900,000 cu ft (25,500 cu m) balloon.
A new, bigger Virgin Global Challenger, a helium and hot air balloon of 1.1 million cu ft (31,100 cu m), was brought to Morocco some six weeks ago, to increase the payload.

Partridge said the balloon, which will fly at a height of around 30,000 to 35,000 ft (9,000-11,000 m), should travel at between 180 and 200 knots, speeds achieved respectively across the Atlantic and the Pacific.

"From Morocco they will enter the sub-tropical jet stream and fly across North Africa, Saudi Arabia and India, where it kinks south, descending to the South China Sea and basically across the Pacific," said Patridge.

"It gets a bit flexible after that, crossing the (United) States anywhere between San Francisco and Seattle, the Rocky Mountains...to land in Kiddlington, Oxford (southern England), which is Branson's hometown."
The flight was estimated to take between 14 and 21 days, with a "realistic" time seen of about 18 days.
The balloon, which will take 12 hours to assemble once the crew has the green light, has never flown before. "You can't test these" without going on the actual flight, McQuillan said.
Marrakesh has been chosen as the ideal launch pad as it is on the faster, southerly sub-tropical jet stream compared with the northern polar jet stream.
Speed is essential -- the Virgin challenge faces a race against American balloonist Steve Fosset and a two-man team planning a launch from Switzerland.

Branson said on Sunday he thought this would be safer than his previous crossing of the Atlantic Ocean because "we will be spending quite some time over land first which will give us time to check out the equipment".

Describing preparations this time, a team member said: "We are trying to make it (conditions in the balloon's capsule) as normal as possible. They are going to have fresh vegetables aboard...They have a micro-wave, and will be taking candy bars and packed food."
Both Branson and Lindstrand have come close to death on previous record-breaking balloon flights in 1987 and 1991, and Branson has termed the bid a "mad adventure".
